Gastroenterology · published research

Anal sphincter injury

Summary of the Evidence

Two randomized animal experiments from the same Iranian research group evaluated 660-nm PBM after surgical anal sphincter injury in rabbits. Each experiment assigned 35 rabbits to five groups of seven and compared PBM alone, a biological adjunct alone, combined treatment, injury control, and an uninjured control. No clinical study was identified (Sarveazad et al. 2019; Sarveazad et al. 2021).

Human and clinical evidence

No human study of PBM for anal sphincter injury was identified. The animal outcomes of sphincter pressure, histology, angiogenesis, and myogenesis do not directly establish continence, symptom relief, safety, or quality-of-life benefit in patients.

Animal evidence

The 2019 experiment compared PBM with human adipose-derived stem cells and their combination. PBM alone improved maximum squeeze pressure and several tissue-repair measures relative to untreated sphincterotomy, while the combined treatment produced stronger results for some functional and structural outcomes (Sarveazad et al. 2019).

The 2021 experiment compared PBM with chondroitinase ABC and their combination. PBM improved resting and squeeze pressure and was associated with less collagen deposition and more muscle and motor units than injury control. The combined treatment exceeded either component alone for several pressure and tissue-repair measures (Sarveazad et al. 2021).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Both experiments used a 660-nm ME-TL10000-SK laser at 100 mW. Treatment was applied immediately after injury and then daily for 14 days. The 2019 protocol delivered 90 seconds per session. The 2021 protocol delivered 30 seconds at each of three points, also totaling 90 seconds per session. Results from a surgical rabbit model and adjunct combinations cannot define effectiveness or an optimal protocol for people.

Interpretation

The two experiments provide a consistent preclinical signal for improved sphincter pressure and tissue repair after PBM, especially in combination groups. Certainty remains very low because both studies were small, came from one research group, used an animal injury model, and did not measure clinical continence or patient-reported outcomes.

Publications and records

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for anal sphincter pressure and tissue repair after experimental injury in rabbits.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Two randomized rabbit experiments from the same research group reported higher sphincter pressures and favorable tissue-repair markers after 660-nm PBM. Each used seven animals per group, and some of the strongest results occurred when PBM was combined with stem cells or chondroitinase ABC. No clinical study has tested continence or patient-reported outcomes, so certainty remains very low.
